stops.name: Kadkan, the village under Nishapur
stops.campa: In the village of Kadkan, in the hill country south of Nishapur, a son is born to a family of some means and named Farid al-Din Muhammad, the pride of the faith. His father keeps the shop of an attar, a druggist and perfumer, and gives the boy an education broader than the trade requires: letters, medicine, the science of simples. The precise year is lost among the shifting dynasties of Khorasan, and scholars argue it by a generation; the tradition of Nishapur fixes it near eleven hundred forty-five, in the last calm years before the earth and the factions both begin to shake.

stops.name: Nishapur, the Street of the Druggists, his father's shop
stops.campa: The family's true home is Nishapur, queen of Khorasan's four capitals, and the shop stands among the apothecaries of the Street of the Druggists, the ʿAttārān, where medicines, perfumes, dyes and spices are weighed out to a city of scholars, merchants and dervishes. As a boy Farid stands at his father's counter learning to grind simples and compound remedies, and to attend the sick who come for more than medicine; from his father's own encouragement he takes an early taste for the sayings of the Sufis passing through the shop, though his hands for now are full of the trade's mortar and pestle.

stops.name: Nishapur, the Street of the Druggists burned
stops.campa: Nishapur in these years is a city eating itself: the old rivalry of the Hanafi and Shafi'i factions, each with its own quarter and its own mob, breaks again into open war in the streets. In the fighting the Street of the Druggists, the ʿAttārān, is deliberately put to the torch, shop upon shop of the trade that gives the family its name. Farid, a boy of perhaps thirteen, watches the quarter of his own inheritance burn among the general ruin of a city that cannot govern its own factions, a first lesson in how quickly a settled world can be undone.

stops.name: Nishapur, the great earthquake
stops.campa: Two years after the burning of the druggists' street, the ground itself turns against the city: a great earthquake shakes Nishapur, toppling minarets and mosques and burying whole neighborhoods a generation had thought permanent. Farid, now some fifteen years old, comes up out of the wreckage of a city that has already survived fire and faction only to be answered by the earth. The tremor and its aftermath settle into him as more than a memory of stone falling; the boy who will one day write the Book of Afflictions has already been given his first affliction to consider.

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the city moves to the garden suburb
stops.campa: In the year after the earthquake, the old walled center of Nishapur is judged beyond saving, and the city's life shifts west to Shadiyakh, the garden suburb of palaces and orchards raised three centuries before by the Tahirid governors. The family's shop reopens here, among the new streets, and it is Shadiyakh, not the ruined old town, that becomes the Nishapur Farid will spend his life in: the ground of his shop, his masterwork, his old age, and, though none can yet know it, of the tomb the centuries will eventually raise a few hundred paces from where he now stands, a boy of sixteen.

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the physicians' bench
stops.campa: Grown into a young man, Farid studies beside the physicians and men of law who cluster around Nishapur's mosques and colleges, the city still famous for its scholars despite all it has suffered. He reads the Arabic of medicine and jurisprudence as the trade demands, but by his own later account it is the sayings of the Sufi masters, heard from boyhood in his father's shop, that hold him more than any formal chair. He signs nothing yet, writes nothing yet; he is a druggist's son finishing his training, indistinguishable, to any stranger passing the shop, from a hundred others of his trade in the city.

stops.name: Shadiyakh, his father's death, the shop his own
stops.campa: His father dies and Farid, still a young man, becomes owner of the shop outright: mortar, scales, the ledger of the ʿAttārān, and the long file of patients who come as much for a kind word as for a remedy. He never again depends on a patron's purse or a court's favor for his bread, a fact he will later be proud enough to set down himself; the trade that named him also frees him, letting him write, when the writing comes, exactly what he pleases and owes to no vizier's taste. For now he only keeps the shop, attends the sick, and grinds his powders.

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the wandering dervish dies at the door
stops.campa: One day, the tradition tells, a wandering dervish comes into the shop and stands looking at the crowded shelves of Farid's trade. He asks the druggist a plain question: whether Farid, for all this, could die as a dervish can. Farid answers, out of the ease of a man who has never been asked, that of course he can. The dervish says nothing more. He sets his begging bowl beneath his head, lies down on the floor of the shop, calls once upon God, and dies there among the mortars and the scales, as easily as a man lying down to sleep, leaving the answer standing in the room.
stops.quote_source: Attar's reply to the dying dervish, in the conversion legend as told by Sholeh Wolpé, 'Attar, the Sufi Poet and Master of Rumi' (World Literature Today)

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the shop closed, the road chosen
stops.campa: The dervish's death at his own threshold does not leave Farid as it found him. He closes the shop, its shelves still full and its customers still standing, and turns from the trade of the body's cures to what he will later call the physic of the soul. He takes the by-name that will outlast his given name, Attar, druggist, and turns it from a trade-mark into a signature under which no shelf of medicine survives but every line of verse does. He sets out, by the report every biographer repeats without ever fixing a date, on the roads of the Sufi world.

stops.name: Bastam, at the tomb of Bayazid
stops.campa: West of Nishapur, on the road toward Iraq and Arabia, Attar turns aside to Bastam, to the tomb of Bayazid al-Bastami, the ecstatic of three centuries before whose sayings on the vanishing of the self into God still scandalize the literal-minded. Attar kneels long at the grave, gathering, as he will gather at every such tomb on this road, the sayings and wonders of the man buried there, for a book of the saints' lives not yet conceived. Of all his subjects it is Bayazid, self-annihilated in the divine, whose voice will echo loudest, decades on, in the mouths of the birds who find the Simurgh is themselves.

stops.name: Kufa, the mosque of Ali
stops.campa: The road continues into Iraq, to Kufa and its great mosque, where the fourth caliph Ali ibn Abi Talib prayed and was struck down at dawn. Attar prays here among pilgrims and scholars from every corner of the Sufi world, listening as much as praying, gathering the stray sentences of dead saints from the mouths of the living who still repeat them. It is a habit that will define his life's second great book: not a poem but a memorial, in plain prose, of every friend of God whose sayings he can still retrieve before the sayings, and the men who carried them, are gone.

stops.name: Mecca, the Hajj
stops.campa: At Mecca, Attar completes the pilgrimage every believer owes, circling the Kaaba among a press of tongues and nations, Persian, Arab, Turk, Berber, at the one point of the earth where all of Islam's roads cross. Between the rites he seeks out the Sufi masters and disciples who winter in the holy city, trading their sayings for his listening, and hears here the name of Mansur al-Hallaj spoken with the particular hush reserved for the executed. He will carry the memory of this circling into the seven valleys his birds must one day cross to reach their own king.
